canberra.title: RBA lifts interest rate for fourth time this year
canberra.snippet: The official interest rate is at its highest since 2011, after the Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.6 per...
canberra.content:
RBA Governor Michele Bullock said the central bank would do what was necessary to bring down inflation. Photo: RBA.

The official interest rate is at its highest since 2011, after the Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.6 per cent.

It will add about $120 a month to the average home loan, bringing this year’s increases to about $480.

The RBA Board voted unanimously on Tuesday (29 September) to increase the rate for a fourth time this year and is prepared to do so again to get inflation under control.

“The board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded,” its statement said.

“To achieve this, growth in aggregate demand needs to remain subdued for a period to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target.

“The three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions and the economy appears to be slowing.

“But inflation is still too high and the board judged that, in light of recent developments, a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support a return of inflation to target in a reasonable period.

“The board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed.”

Global uncertainty, including the Middle East war and AI-related demands, were contributing factors to the RBA’s decision.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers homed in on that point and said Australians had been placed under pressure and were paying a hefty price because of the conflict overseas.

“The Reserve Bank statement makes it really clear that we have an inflation challenge in our economy, which is made worse by the war in the Middle East,” he said.

“The statement makes it abundantly clear that one of the main drivers of inflation in our economy is a conflict on the other side of the world, pushing up global oil prices and being felt right around our economy and indeed right around the world.

“The war in the Middle East is not the only factor when it comes to our inflation challenge, but it is a very, very big factor.

“Australians are paying a very hefty price for that war in the Middle East. And today that price became a bit steeper with this decision from the independent Reserve Bank.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the outcome as terrible for the nation.

He said Labor had worsened the pressure on Australians and increased inflation through excessive government spending.

“This is a dark day, a tough day for hardworking Australian families with a mortgage, those in small businesses, but more particularly households who have got a mortgage who are going to pay more as a result of this $1400 a year in additional costs,” Mr Taylor said.

“We know that this is a government that is spending too much. We also know it’s an economy that is not working and that drives up inflation and it drives up interest rates.

“Labor’s spending has been much faster than the overall economy. Households and families are having to tighten their belts, but the government hasn’t tightened its belt and that drives up inflation and interest rates, and all Australians are paying a price for that.”

Some Coalition members are now calling for Labor to “redo” its federal budget.

RBA Governor Michele Bullock spoke to the media about an hour after the board’s decision was announced and said the central bank would continue to do what was required to rein in inflation.

She said higher interest rates were needed to ensure inflation returned to the cash target, but the hikes so far this year may be sufficient.

“We raised interest rates three times earlier in the year. A lot of that effect is still to flow through. This is one more,” Ms Bullock said.

“What we are predicting here is that this will be restrictive enough. Those interest rate increases bring things down …

“Now, I know this decision is difficult for households with a mortgage and businesses with loans, but high inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable.

“Every household has seen how the price of everything has gone up in recent years. Pay packets don’t go as far as they used to, and that’s why we need to stop this high inflation.”

canberra.title: Former drug dealer says arrest helped him break free of addiction
canberra.snippet: A former drug dealer caught with nearly $20,000-worth of illegal substances has thanked authorities for arresting him, saying it helped h...
canberra.content:
29 September 2026

Leba Anthony Awad, 55, has been sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court over drug offences. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A former drug dealer caught with nearly $20,000-worth of illegal substances has thanked authorities for arresting him, saying it helped him break free of his own drug addiction.

Leba Anthony Awad was sentenced to nearly 300 days in jail by the ACT Supreme Court last week, backdated to account for the time he already spent behind bars.

This means the 55-year-old has served his sentence and was not returned to custody.

Acting Justice James Stewart, in his recently published decision, said police were searching for a different person over an unrelated matter when they went to the Brighton apartment complex in Kingston on 27 January 2025.

Police went to Awad’s apartment and explained they were looking for this person, so he invited the officers in to search his home for them.

But once the officers went inside, they became suspicious that he may be dealing drugs himself.

A search of his apartment found meth, cannabis, scales and a large quantity of unused clip-seal bags. Police went on to raid his home on 7 February 2025 and found more drugs.

In total, police found 27 grams of meth worth $7200, 610 grams of cannabis worth $5100, 16 grams of MDMA worth $4740 and $2595 cash.

“[The] combined weights, value (a total of $17,040) and repetition of the presence of the substances speak to low-level ongoing dealing at the time of the offending,” Acting Justice Stewart said.

“The purposes of the offending were the support of the offender’s illicit drug use and funding his day-to-day living expenses.

“There was no evidence of a grandiose lifestyle or any type of sophistication or syndication of sale.”

The acting justice said the court recognised the insidious nature of illicit drugs and the devastating effect they can have on individuals.

“The court regularly observes the consequential ripple effects of illicit drug trafficking throughout the community,” he said.

But he said Awad had taken full responsibility for his offending. He said he was in the grip of addiction at the time of the offending and was making poor choices, but after he was released from custody he undertook residential rehabilitation in NSW.

“[The] offender expressed thanks for being arrested as it caused him to address his addiction which in turn addressed his offending behaviour,” the judge said.

Acting Justice Stewart said Awad was unemployed but was studying for a diploma, undertaking counselling and had adopted a changed attitude that helped him maintain a positive mindset.

“He is a man who has contributed to the recovery of others in the past and was previously part of a focus working group that assisted the creation of the Drug and Alcohol Sentencing List in this court,” he said.

Awad spent 272 days in custody before he was released in November 2025 on restrictive bail conditions that allowed for residential rehabilitation.

“The offender has travelled a long way on his personal journey since the offending,” Acting Justice Stewart said.

“Given the actual rehabilitation that has been completed and the fact that there has been more time in custody served than required, I concluded that there was and is no requirement for a good behaviour order.”

Awad had pleaded guilty to trafficking meth and MDMA.

canberra.title: Murderer admits he ‘tortured’ partner while savagely killing her
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content and refers to family violence. A murderer has denied he intended to kill his p...
canberra.content:
Tiffany Marie Spence was killed by her partner in 2022. Photo: Supplied by family.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content and refers to family violence.

A murderer has denied he intended to kill his partner when she was trying to leave their relationship, but admitted he wanted to torture her as punishment with a savage beating.

“What’s with the tone?” Adam James Britt asked ACT Director of Public Prosecutions Victoria Engel SC during a frequently tense cross-examination on Tuesday (29 September).

“I’m getting confused about everything … She’s getting angry at me.”

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum remarked, “I don’t think you’re confused at all”.

Britt was arrested five months after he killed 36-year-old Tiffany Marie Spence at their home in September 2022, before pleading guilty to murder in the week he was scheduled to face trial.

Region then obtained court documents about the case, showing an autopsy found bruises or other injuries had covered 40 per cent of Ms Spence’s body.

These injuries would have likely killed her on their own, but she also had rib and spinal fractures, extensive injuries to her neck and a collapsed lung.

The documents contain many details that are too distressing to publish.

Britt testified himself when his sentencing hearing continued in the ACT Supreme Court on Tuesday because he was arguing he did not intend to kill Ms Spence.

Under cross-examination from Ms Engel, the 41-year-old claimed he didn’t know Ms Spence had been trying to leave their relationship when he killed her.

He was shown photos depicting the sickening injuries he left on her body.

“You beat her to such a pulp that she had injuries to 40 per cent of her body,” Ms Engel said before asking what was going through his mind at the time.

“Several different things … I don’t know, I can’t explain,” he answered.

He claimed their relationship had been “going okay” even though Ms Spence disappeared for almost a week just before he murdered her.

He admitted he was angry at her because she disappeared and he felt like she lied to him. He accepted he was in “a rage” and wanted to “punish” her, although he denied he wanted to punish her because she was trying to leave him.

“The only intention that you must have had would be to kill her,” Ms Engel argued.

“No,” he replied.

The court heard that while repeatedly beating Ms Spence, he stopped to download pornography.

“With your partner lying in the state that you beat her to, with your partner covered in blood, you downloaded pornography, Mr Britt?” Ms Engel asked.

“Did you take pleasure in the injuries you caused to Tiffany, Mr Britt? Did it give you a sexual kick?”

“No,” he replied. He also said she wasn’t dead when he downloaded the pornography, although she was in “a relatively bad state”.

Ms Engel also asked why he planted a hammer in Ms Spence’s hand after killing her.

“I don’t really know what I was thinking. I think I was just panicking,” he said.

The court heard that Britt took photos of the injuries he was leaving on Ms Spence’s body during the beating.

When questioned by Chief Justice McCallum, he admitted he did this because he wanted to be able to show his partner what happened when he got angry.

The Chief Justice asked if he thought continuing to punish Ms Spence more and more over two-and-a-half days amounted to “a form of torture”.

“Yes,” he replied.

Afterwards, Ms Engel asked for the court to impose a life sentence for Britt, partly due to the “terrifying and tortuous manner of Tiffany’s death”.

She said Ms Spence had been trying to escape the relationship and find somewhere else to live before Britt killed her.

“He then attempts to blame Ms Spence for her own death … in a calculated fashion over many years,” she said.

Barrister Philip Massey said it was “a very, very grave and disturbing murder”, but the issue was what his client’s intention was at the time of the beating.

He said that as his client took photos of Ms Spence during the beating to show to her in the future, this demonstrated he intended to cause grievous bodily harm, not kill her.

“There would be no point in taking the photos if she would not survive,” Mr Massey argued.

Chief Justice McCallum will sentence Britt, who remains in custody, in December.

canberra.title: Accused groomer allegedly sent sexual messages to 14-year-old girl, left her cash
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A man allegedly spent months grooming a young girl, including messaging her ...
canberra.content:
Police allege 23-year-old Rami Saleh had been messaging a 14-year-old girl over social media. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A man allegedly spent months grooming a young girl, including messaging her over social media and hiding cash for her to collect, before he was arrested.

Rami Saleh, a 23-year-old from the ACT suburb of Farrer, was remanded in custody after his arrest, then spent three weeks behind bars before applying for bail on Tuesday (29 September).

The ACT Magistrates Court heard it alleged he sent numerous sexual messages to a 14-year-old girl over about four months earlier in 2026.

In addition, he allegedly left her money, sent her child abuse material, gave her alcohol and cash in person and asked to see her alone.

Mr Saleh pleaded not guilty to charges of grooming a young person, using a carriage service for child abuse material and supplying liquor to a young person.

The prosecutor, when opposing his bail application on Tuesday, argued his alleged offences were persistent as they continued for about four months.

She alleged Mr Saleh messaged the girl over social media apps Instagram and Snapchat, and that his actions involved a level of secrecy. For instance, he allegedly hid cash for the girl in bushes.

The court heard that police were still reviewing his electronic devices and thought it would take another four weeks to complete the process.

“In particular, in relation to the evidence, once it is gone, it is gone,” the prosecutor said, after saying much of the evidence was on social media apps.

She said the girl had expressed concerns to police about the welfare of herself and her brother, who Mr Saleh was also alleged to have met, if he was granted bail.

But barrister Anthony Williamson SC said his client had complied with police orders regarding his electronic devices, and he argued investigators should have the relevant data by now.

“If they haven’t done so, with respect, that is a them problem,” he said.

“He’s been in custody for weeks now.

“So if this has not been attended to by now, it ought to have been.”

Mr Williamson also argued that any claim his client could interfere with evidence if granted bail was speculative.

Magistrate Ian Temby was concerned about the alleged risks of Mr Saleh interfering with witnesses or reoffending, given the nature of the allegations and some of the material found on his phone.

But he agreed with Mr Williamson’s submissions that the risk of him deleting evidence from social media was speculative, and that police had had the opportunity to obtain the evidence they needed.

Magistrate Temby granted bail on several strict conditions, including that Mr Saleh reside under a curfew, be supervised by authorities, not contact the girl or her family, not leave the ACT and have only one phone, which police can inspect.

The matter was adjourned to 22 October.

In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

canberra.title: One tree or one more apartment? Canberra confronts the cost of a green canopy
canberra.snippet: A promised 10-day pathway to resolve tree disputes holding up Canberra housing projects may not be as quick as it sounds, with Master Bui...
canberra.content:
A question for a city being asked to build more homes within its existing footprint: what happens to our trees? Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A promised 10-day pathway to resolve tree disputes holding up Canberra housing projects may not be as quick as it sounds, with Master Builders ACT warning the clock could be repeatedly reset and applicants left carrying thousands of dollars in specialist costs.

The industry body has backed the ACT Government’s attempt to give builders and homeowners earlier answers on whether a protected tree can be removed, but says the proposed process could still be lengthy and expensive.

Under the Urban Forest and Planning Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, decisions on removing protected trees for design reasons could be made separately from the full development application process.

Master Builders told a Legislative Assembly inquiry the proposed 10-working-day assessment period could restart when officials sought further information.

“The principal one is in fact around the legislative timeframe, which is the 10 days which can be stopped and reset continuously,” CEO Anna Neelegama told the inquiry.

“If you reset it on day 10 and you do that 100 times, you therefore attract a 100-day delay.”

Master Builders also argued much of the work required from applicants would remain unchanged. In its submission it argues that plans, design material and specialist evidence will still be needed, including an arborist’s report it says typically costs between $5000 and $10,000 for each tree proposed for removal.

“The only part this legislation’s really changing is putting the 10-day limit on the government,” it added.

Government officials rejected concerns that the timeframe would prove difficult to meet, saying an existing comparable process consistently meets a 10-day deadline.

The new assessment would be limited to the proposed design, the tree and relevant supporting information rather than requiring the referrals, public notification and broader assessment involved in a full 35-day development application.

“We think that that’s very achievable to do within that 10 days and the team have relevant experience in delivering on that time frame,” an official said.

But behind the argument about how many days an approval should take sits a much bigger question for a city being asked to build more homes within its existing footprint: what happens when the tree is standing where those homes need to go?

Property Council ACT and Capital Region executive director Ashley Berry said uncertainty around trees could emerge after developers had already spent considerable time and money progressing a project.

Developers could spend “12, 18 months or more” going through the development application process before being told a tree could not be removed, potentially forcing them to redesign the project or change the number of homes proposed.

The Property Council said it supported the Bill, but wanted decisions made early enough for developers to know what could realistically be built on a site.

“We’re constantly going to be weighing up, you know, is this tree worth homes,” Ms Berry said.

Ms Berry acknowledged that if delivering housing were the only consideration, the answer would be straightforward.

“How can we get the balance right between maintaining the trees that we need and also delivering housing?”

The government’s proposed guidelines attempt to draw that line.

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel told the inquiry a tree’s position on a block would be relevant. A tree sitting in the middle of a block could fall within its primary building zone and potentially be considered for removal.

The draft guidelines also list a development delivering additional homes and a mixture of dwelling types and sizes within the existing urban footprint as a characteristic that could favour removing a protected tree.

Climate Change, Environment, Energy and Water Minister Suzanne Orr said the assessment would go well beyond counting additional homes.

A tree’s species, condition, life expectancy, location and ecological value would be considered alongside the consequences of the proposed design. Applicants would also have to consider reasonable alternatives that could allow the tree to remain.

“Is there a better design outcome that retains the tree and if not, are other objectives going to be met that justify its removal?” Ms Orr said.

Registered, remnant and heritage trees would not be covered by the new pathway.

The Conservation Council ACT Region nevertheless warned that the reforms risked making it easier to sacrifice mature trees for additional housing.

The council supports greater urban density but described the idea that Canberra must choose between densification and its urban forest as a “false” choice.

It is particularly concerned about the meaning of a “desired planning outcome”, arguing the concept could allow a developer to point to missing-middle housing objectives to justify removing mature trees.

It said mature native trees deserved a strong presumption in favour of retention because some can take 100 to 150 years to replace.

The inquiry also established that the government has not specifically modelled the impact the Bill could have on Canberra’s tree canopy.

Greens MLA Andrew Braddock asked whether analysis had been undertaken to determine whether the changes could be detrimental to canopy cover compared with the existing legislation, to which Ms Orr replied: “No, not against the bill.”

She added that separate modelling was being developed to examine different scenarios for reaching the government’s 30 per cent canopy target, part of the government’s new climate policy.

City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said the legislation was not creating a new choice between development and trees. Planning decisions can already allow a tree to be removed through the DA process.

“What we’ve sought to do with the amendments in this bill … is to make that a stand-alone process, rather than having it as part of a DA,” she said.

“So it can be brought forward in the development cycle, you can also then scrutinize that process quite a bit more.”

Ms Cheyne said the change would not allow trees to be removed that could not already be considered for removal, but would bring the decision forward and make the process more transparent.

australia.title: Imams’ council condemns Melbourne Islamic preacher’s call to ‘take up arms’ against enemies
australia.snippet: Independent MP Allegra Spender says the comments reinforce the need for stronger protection against hate speech Get our breaking news ema...
australia.content:
Australia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”.

The Australian National Imams’ Council (ANIC) released a statement on Tuesday after Nine newspapers revealed the preacher who goes by the name Abu Ahmad made the comments during a sermon in July.

Reading from a book chapter, Ahmad said Muslims should not “take the Jews and the Christians for friends” in a video posted to the social media feed of Melbourne-based Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre in July.

“For the sake of Allah, it includes the obligation to declare enmity for his sake, opposition for the sake of Allah. It is to declare opposition, indeed, to take up arms against his enemies, to shun them, and to stay far from them both in word and deed. This proves that simple opposition of the spirit is not enough and that it must be complete by honouring of your commitment,” he said.

“If the aim of the enemies of Islam, whether they are atheists, or Jews, or Christians, or modernists, or Zionists, or communists, is the emasculation of … the Muslims and the erosion of their unique character in order to make them the ass of the chosen people, as it is put in the protocols of the elders of Zion, then the urgency of this issue should become clear to every Muslim,” he said.

In an Instagram post on Monday, the Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre included a statement from the preacher.

“The statements the article is attributing to me were from a passage of a book that I was reading during a lesson on al-Walāʾ wal-Barāʾ. They were not a personal call from me for Muslims to attack Christians, Jews or other non-Muslims,” the post signed off by Ahmad said.

The post attached a video which he said was an “explanation of that very passage from the same lesson” and explained it “does not permit harming, oppressing or being unjust towards peaceful non-Muslims.

“Unfortunately, quoting the book without including the explanation that followed gives a completely different impression of what was being taught,” the post said.

ANIC said it “strongly and unequivocally condemns any call by any religious or non-religious preacher, leader or individual to take up arms against civilians, religious communities or the Australian people”.

ANIC said it would not make findings about the “individual or the precise context of the reported remarks” until it could properly review material.

ANIC reiterated it “categorically rejects incitement to violence, hatred or harm against any person or community”.

“The safety, security and wellbeing of Australia and the Australian people are fundamental responsibilities that Australian Muslims, Imams and religious leaders must uphold. Islamic teachings require Muslims to honour the sanctity of human life, fulfil their responsibilities to society and contribute positively to the communities and country in which they live.”

The peak body called on all religious leaders, regardless of faith, to exercise responsibility in their public statements. It added that the alleged conduct of an individual should not be used to condemn or blame an entire faith or community.

The Albanese government was forced to abandon anti-vilification laws that would have given authorities greater powers to crack down on religious leaders who promote hatred on the basis of religions, race, gender or sexuality after it failed to gain support from the Nationals and the Greens.

On Tuesday, the independent federal MP Allegra Spender told Nine newspapers the comments showed “why we needed stronger and nationally consistent hate speech legislation”.

australia.title: Revealed: the five-paragraph email OpenAI used to inform Australia about agent attack
australia.snippet: Executive to front parliamentary committee on AI as ministers reveal how brief message telling them about hack was signed off ‘best’ Foll...
australia.content:
OpenAI has apologised to Australians for its agent attack on Medicare, and will front parliament next week as the tech company revealed more details about its June hack of Australian government websites.

Ministers on Tuesday evening released a brief, five paragraph email which OpenAI used to inform the Australian government about the attack. The email was sent to a public inbox monitored by Services Australia on 10 September – nearly three months after the AI agent accessed the website on 18 June – and was signed off with the closing “best”.

The Labor government has publicly voiced its fury at the manner in which OpenAI disclosed the incident. The email itself, obtained by Guardian Australia, advised Services Australia that “an OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password”.

In a blog post released on Tuesday morning (Aest), OpenAI said it should have handled its response better.

“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”

The company also provided more detail on the incident revealed by the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, last week.

OpenAI said it became aware of agent activity on Australian government websites in mid-August after the company reviewed earlier training incidents after the Hugging Face attack in July.

The agents gained non-public access to a Services Australia portal for Medicare statistics, and OpenAI said the agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files, but no patient or client records were accessed.

OpenAI’s email to Services Australia pointed the government to the “affected URL”, a Medicare statistics page on the human services website, as well as specifying an “affected report” – a CSV file, commonly used for spreadsheets.

“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available,” OpenAI wrote.

“Best, OpenAl Security Team”.

OpenAI was contacted for comment.

The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research’s public crime mapping tool was also accessed, with application configuration, operational jobs and logs and website metadata provided to the agency.

The agent discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian agency for health information’s reporting system to access aggregate survey statistics.

For the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, OpenAI agents retrieved aggregate statistics, but separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful and the information obtained was publicly available.

Services Australia and the Victorian health department were informed on 10 September, while the NSW bureau of crime stastistics was informed on 18 September.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare was not informed until 24 September, as OpenAI deemed it did not meet disclosure thresholds.

“Since then we’ve worked closely with Australian government agencies to share what we’ve learned to date,” OpenAI said. “If we identify any additional affected agencies, we will notify them promptly and directly with the information available and provide updates as further facts emerge.”

The incident occurred after one model was tasked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victoria. The model had difficulty obtaining that information, and OpenAI said “it took actions that we had not authorised it to take” including accessing Services Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service.

OpenAI said it would commit resources and expertise to affected agencies, and provide Australian government agencies with support to build cyberdefences on critical infrastructure.

Australian government agencies and industries will also be given credits out of OpenAI’s US$1bn (AU$1.4bn) Daybreak fund, which lets those organisations use frontier AI for cyberdefence, and to harden their systems by reviewing code and system configurations for potential vulnerabilities that can then be patched.

The company said it would also establish a taskforce with Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations on managing risk with AI agents.

OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will appear at the joint select committee on AI on Tuesday 6 October. Guardian Australia reported on Monday that Anthropic would also appear at this hearing, but not at a Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres this week.

Albanese, who was in the United States last week when he announced the hack, said at the time he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”.

On Tuesday, Albanese said OpenAI had been “very constructive and open in engaging” since the incident, as had Anthropic. He said AI can improve economic growth and productivity but it also carries risks.

“And we’ve seen those risks exposed – not just in what occurred in Australia, but the revelation that has occurred in the United States and other countries as well.”

The federal government has flagged it could introduce mandatory reporting rules for AI-related data breaches, after the revelation OpenAI used a public-facing email address three months after the hack to report the incident to Services Australia.

The company said on Tuesday it had “a lot of work ahead” to rebuild trust with Australians but said it was making “meaningful changes”.

australia.title: Sydney teen taken to hospital after falling from moving bus on northern beaches
australia.snippet: Transport for NSW, bus operator and Rail, Tram and Bus union investigate after incident on Monday evening Get our breaking news email , f...
australia.content:
Investigations are under way after a teenage girl fell from a moving double-decker bus on to a busy road in Sydney’s northern beaches.

Emergency services were called to Manly Road at Seaforth on Monday evening after the teenager fell from the B-Line bus near the Spit Bridge.

She was treated at the scene for head and hip injuries and taken to Royal North Shore hospital, where a spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday she remained in a stable condition.

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said it was aware of the incident on Spit Road and that the bus had been withdrawn from service while an investigation by bus operator Keolis Northern Beaches and the department takes place.

“The passenger was treated at the scene and taken to hospital with minor injuries,” they said. “We wish the passenger all the best in her recovery.”

The incident has also been reported to the Office of Transport Safety Investigations.

On Tuesday, the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) said Keolis Northern Beaches, “must urgently explain how a door on one of its B-Line buses reportedly failed” and that it was investigating reports from drivers that doors on the fleet had opened unexpectedly in the past.

RTBU NSW Tram and Bus Division secretary Peter Grech said private operator Keolis and Transport for NSW must “come clean” about whether warnings had been ignored.

“A 16-year-old girl fell out of a moving bus … onto one of the Northern Beaches’ busiest roads. It is horrifying to think how much worse this could have been,” Grech said. “She should have been safe on that bus and this was undoubtedly a highly traumatic experience for her.

“Drivers are telling us this may not be the first time one of these doors has opened unexpectedly. We are currently checking the circumstances, but Keolis cannot leave passengers wondering whether there were warnings it simply failed to act on.

“If a door can open while a bus is moving, then that bus cannot be carrying the public,” he said.

Keolis responded to Guardian Australia’s request for comment on Tuesday afternoon with a statement confirming it was “aware of an incident that occurred last night on our B-Line service which resulted in a passenger falling from the bus near the Spit Bridge at Seaforth”.

“Our immediate thoughts are with the passenger and her family and wishing for a swift recovery.”

It is understood Bustech double-decker B-Line buses have been taken out of service, although Keolis and Transport for NSW have not confirmed which vehicles were withdrawn or when.

It has not been established when and how earlier concerns were reported to Keolis management, the response drivers received or what steps were taken to control the risk.

It is understood the union is seeking records from Keolis and Transport for NSW under the work health and safety act as part of its investigation.

australia.title: Danger zone: why war in the Middle East has landed the RBA’s inflation fight in tricky territory
australia.snippet: The Reserve Bank appears ready to push harder against inflation but it comes with a greater risk for the economy The fight against inflat...
australia.content:
The fight against inflation has entered a new, more dangerous phase.

For years, the Reserve Bank has been attempting, as gently as possible, to steer inflation back to its 2.5% target while trying to retain as many of the post-pandemic job gains as possible.

“That still remains the strategy,” Michele Bullock, the RBA’s governor, told journalists on Tuesday afternoon, an hour after the board announced the fourth interest rate hike for the year.

Unemployment has climbed by 1 percentage point over the past four years, sure, but at 4.6% it’s “still quite low historically,” Bullock said.

Other central banks have managed to get inflation lower, sure, but at the cost of higher unemployment, she said.

Yet there are signs that the central bank may be losing faith in this “slowly, slowly” strategy.

Bullock explained the RBA has been outside the 2-3% target range for six years now. That’s a problem, because households and businesses need to believe that inflation will fall again, one day.

“We came in [to the range] briefly in 2025, and then we’ve popped back out again. We are aiming to get it back,” she said.

But how to get inflation back under control “in a reasonable time”, when unreasonable things keep happening?

It’s the unending Middle East conflict that now looms as the biggest threat to the RBA’s careful approach to taming inflation.

As Bullock said: “When the Middle East conflict first started, everyone was sort of thinking, ‘Oh, it will probably not last very long’.”

“Well, that’s clearly not true. It’s lasted, and there doesn’t seem to be any end to it,” she said.

Fuel prices, fertiliser prices, transport prices are now all “permanently higher”.

“So this idea that they would go up and then come down again just hasn’t happened.”

The RBA governor is worried that businesses are also coming to the same conclusion, and will start lifting their prices. That will make it even harder to get inflation back to target without a more dramatic increase in interest rates.

Bullock and her board have long made it clear they will “do what it takes” to get inflation back to target, a phrase they repeated on Tuesday.

After Tuesday’s announcement, a number of economists are betting the RBA will hike again in six weeks’ time, at the Melbourne Cup day meeting. Financial markets see a 50% chance of yet another increase next year.

All up, it sounds like the RBA is ready to start pushing harder against inflation.

That might be the right call, but it increases the risk the central bank will push too hard and, in Bullock’s words, drive the economy into a “dramatic slowdown”.

“Hopefully, in the next couple of years, when we get inflation back down, this will have all been worth it.”

australia.title: New fees, higher costs: Card surcharges are ending – how will it affect the way you pay?
australia.snippet: Australian ban on credit and debit card surcharges begins this week. Businesses plan to pass the cost on to consumers – or avoid it altog...
australia.content:
Australians will no longer pay a surcharge on credit or debit card purchases from Thursday, but the changes at the register won’t stop there.

Some businesses are already making changes, with an after-school care provider cutting off card payments and a school canteen service setting $10 minimum checkouts to manage processing costs.

At the same time, major banks and card providers are trimming cardholder benefits to offset their own expenses.

The result is a series of swift rule changes as businesses decide how to handle fees they are no longer permitted to pass on to customers.

A return to cash?

The Reserve Bank says businesses that wish to steer consumers towards other payment methods can do so by providing discounts instead of using surcharges.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has issued similar advice, saying that businesses can offer discounts to consumers who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID.

In 2025, about 15% of payments were made in cash and around half of Australians used cash in a typical week, according to the RBA. There had been a slight increase in the number of people who carried cash – from 47% in 2022 to 50% in 2025. This was the first time the number of people using cash had increased since the RBA started its monitoring in 2007.

Jason Bryce from Cash Welcome, a group that advocates cash usage, expects cash transactions to become more common again after the end of surcharging. Bryce says it will become more typical to see small businesses display “cash preferred” or “discounts for cash” signage at the point of sale.

“Other countries that have a history of banning card surcharges have a lot more cash-only businesses [and] a lot more cash-preferred businesses,” he says.

France, Germany, Japan and Korea, which have all banned surcharges, have more cash in circulation and more merchants accepting cash than Australia, Bryce says.

No more card payments

Prof Steve Worthington of Swinburne university, a payment systems expert, says many merchants “have not decided how they want to play this”.

“We’ll have to wait and see whether merchants just increase their prices to compensate for the lack of surcharging or whether they stick with their normal pricing and try to raise money other ways,” he says.

Worthington believes there will be more cash used in the economy after Thursday, as well as more businesses asking consumers to pay via direct debit.

The RBA says businesses and other merchants are generally able to choose which payment methods they accept, which can include adding new payment methods and withdrawing existing payment methods.

Guardian Australia is aware of several merchants who have already informed customers they will stop accepting card payments altogether. For example, the Cubby out of school hours care service has written to families telling them that, “due to the new laws regarding credit card fees, Cubby OOSH has decided to no longer accept credit or debit cards as the payment method”. The company was contacted for comment.

Extra fees and other new rules

Sally Tindall, the data insights director at financial comparison site Canstar, says businesses are in a difficult position, because they’ll have to absorb the costs associated with processing fees, or pass them on through higher prices.

“That’s a difficult decision for lots of businesses,” she says. “And for some businesses, it’ll be a matter of doing a bit of both, absorbing some of the costs and passing some of the costs on.”

Flexischools, an online ordering platform for school canteens, activities and uniforms – which says it is used by 25% of all Australian parents – has told families it will incorporate the costs that had been covered by surcharges into the fees they pay for the service.

In an email to families on 22 September, seen by Guardian Australia, Flexischools said it was introducing a $10 minimum at checkout, “to help manage the cost of processing small payments”, even if an order – such as a canteen item – is less than $10, with any balance to be saved for later use. Additionally, Flexischools said its online order fees would increase by 6c per transaction.

Flexischools told Guardian Australia the additional 6c per online order would “cover processing”. The company said it expected that, on average, parents would pay less under the new fee structure than what they had paid with a surcharge.

“Flexischools has a range of different pricing structures and services available, so this may vary by school,” the company said.

To help businesses absorb the costs, the RBA will further limit interchange fees – which the merchant’s bank pays to the customer’s card issuer to cover the cost of processing the payment. But fees for payment networks cannot be escaped altogether.

“For a small business, there is no such thing as a cost that simply disappears,” says Skye Cappuccio, the chief executive of the industry peak body, Cosboa.

“Every business is different. Some may be able to absorb some or all of the cost, while others may need to review their overall pricing or payment arrangements.”

world.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
world.snippet: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says A senior member of t...
world.content:
A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.

The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.

Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.

Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
world.snippet: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue...
world.content:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.

Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
world.snippet: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s c...
world.content:
Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.

In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.

Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.

Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
world.snippet: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a retu...
world.content:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”

The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.

In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.

The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.

AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
world.snippet: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s ...
world.content:
A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.

The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.

Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.

Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.

“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”

Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”

Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.

Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.

Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.

Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.

The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.

Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.
